merge-sort.title: Merge sort · small pieces, one ordered row

scenes.heading: Which number comes first?
scenes.caption: Merge sort, one small decision at a time.
scenes.narration: Which number belongs first? One. But how could a program find every next number without searching the whole row again?

scenes.heading: Make the problem smaller.
scenes.caption: Two halves. The same values.
scenes.narration: Start with two smaller problems. Split the row in half. Nothing has changed order yet.

scenes.heading: Make the problem smaller.
scenes.caption: Then split each half.
scenes.narration: Split each half again. Now we only need to put a pair of numbers in order.

scenes.heading: One number is already sorted.
scenes.caption: This is where the splitting stops.
scenes.narration: Split once more. A number on its own is already sorted. Now we can build back up.

scenes.heading: Let the smaller number lead.
scenes.caption: Compare the neighbours, then build each pair.
scenes.narration: Three beats seven. Two beats eight. On each side, copy the smaller number first. Then let the other follow.

scenes.heading: Bring the ordered pairs back.
scenes.caption: Each pair returns to its place.
scenes.narration: Put each finished pair back where it belongs. We have four little rows that are already in order.

scenes.heading: Watch the front of each group.
scenes.caption: Blue = left input · Mint = right input
scenes.narration: Here, two beats three, while one beats four. Then compare the next fronts. Only the side we took from moves forward.

scenes.heading: Two halves, ready to join.
scenes.caption: Sorted within each half—not across the whole row yet.
scenes.narration: Each half is ready. The numbers inside it are ordered, but the whole row still needs joining.

scenes.heading: Why are the fronts enough?
scenes.caption: Nothing behind either front can be smaller.
scenes.narration: Now watch: one, then two, then three. We only look at the fronts, because nothing behind them can be smaller. When one side runs out, the rest follows.

scenes.heading: Bring the finished row home.
scenes.caption: The ordered result returns to the original row.
scenes.narration: Now put the finished row back. Every number has found its place, from one through eight.

scenes.heading: Small pieces. One ordered row.
scenes.caption: Split it down. Build it back in order.
scenes.narration: That is merge sort. Make small sorted pieces, then let their fronts guide you to a bigger sorted row.

scenes.heading: Same input. Different work.
scenes.caption: Height = value. Position = index.
scenes.narration: These bars show the array seven, three, five, two. Height means value. Position means index. Bubble, selection and insertion can reach the same sorted result, but their intermediate movements are different.

scenes.heading: Bubble: exchange neighbours
scenes.caption: 7 travels right through three adjacent swaps.
scenes.narration: Bubble compares neighbouring values. Seven swaps with three, then five, then two. After this complete pass, seven is final on the right. The rest is not sorted yet: five still comes before two.

scenes.heading: Selection: scan first, swap once
scenes.caption: Select index 3. Then swap 7 ↔ 2.
scenes.narration: Selection scans the entire unsorted range without moving its bars. It remembers the smallest value, two, at index three. When the scan finishes, one distant swap exchanges two and seven. Index zero is now final.

scenes.heading: Insertion: hold, shift, insert
scenes.caption: Sorted prefix [3,5,7]. Hold key 2.
scenes.narration: For insertion, this example starts with the sorted prefix three, five, seven. Hold the next key, two, outside the array. Shift seven right, then five, then three. Put two into the gap. These are one way shifts and a final insertion, not swaps.

scenes.heading: Count the operation, not just the answer
scenes.caption: A comparison, a swap and a write are different counts.
scenes.narration: For these illustrated operations, bubble makes three comparisons and three swaps. Selection makes three comparisons and one swap. Inserting two into three sorted values makes three comparisons, three shifts and one insertion. State the counting convention before reporting a total.

scenes.heading: Linear search works without sorting
scenes.caption: Check indexes 0, 1, 2. Return index 2.
scenes.narration: Linear search checks one position at a time. To find five here, inspect seven, then three, then five. Return index two, not the value five. Stop at the first match. No array value moves.

scenes.heading: Binary search needs sorted input
scenes.caption: Ascending order makes discarding a half valid.
scenes.narration: Binary search depends on sorted order. In this ascending array, the midpoint is index two, holding five. We are searching for seven. Because five is too small, every value at or before that midpoint is also too small.

scenes.heading: Discard the failed midpoint too
scenes.caption: low = mid + 1 = 3 · high stays 4
scenes.narration: Set low to mid plus one, which is three. High stays four. The next midpoint is three, holding seven, so return three. We discarded candidates. We did not move, swap, or delete array elements.

scenes.heading: What if the key is absent?
scenes.caption: Inclusive bounds: continue while low ≤ high.
scenes.narration: For a missing key, continue until the candidate interval is empty. Searching for six probes five, then seven. Low becomes three and high becomes two. Bounds crossed, so return minus one. A single remaining candidate must still be checked.

scenes.heading: Choose from the data you already have
lines: One query in unsorted data → linear
Repeated queries in sorted data → binary
Search result = index; not the matching value
scenes.caption: Account for preprocessing and preserve original indexes.
scenes.narration: For one search in unsorted data, a linear scan avoids unnecessary sorting. For many searches in already sorted array data, binary search is useful. Remember: sorting can change original positions. Do not silently return a sorted index when the question asks for the original index.

scenes.heading: A package is a class address
scenes.caption: The declaration defines identity.
scenes.narration: A package gives a type a qualified address. Package school dot people, class Student, means school dot people dot Student. Moving the source file alone does not change that identity. The declaration does.

scenes.heading: An import is a shorter spelling
lines: No installation. No file copying. No access override.
scenes.caption: Imports affect name resolution in one source file.
scenes.narration: An import lets one source file use Student as a short name. It does not install the class, copy its source, or grant access to a hidden constructor. A wildcard imports types directly in one package, not its subpackages.

scenes.heading: Source root and output root differ
scenes.caption: Source lookup → compilation → generated bytecode
scenes.narration: Below the source root, folders mirror the package. The compiler reads dot java files and writes dot class files. The d option chooses the output root. Sourcepath chooses where source dependencies can be found. They have different jobs.

scenes.heading: Launch from the root above the package
scenes.caption: Use the qualified main-class name, without .class.
scenes.narration: To run school dot app dot Main, point the classpath at classes, the root above school. Java appends the package path and class filename. Pointing at classes slash school repeats school in the lookup path. Run the qualified name without the dot class extension.

scenes.heading: Repair the failing layer
lines: Main method not found → entry point
scenes.caption: More imports cannot fix every failure.
scenes.narration: Diagnose the layer before changing code. Cannot find symbol suggests a name or lookup problem. Not public is an access problem. Main method not found means the selected class was found, but the required entry point is missing. More imports cannot repair all three.
